submission.clinical_question: Does hysterosalpingography demonstrate intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) or cervical stenosis causing secondary amenorrhea and cyclic pelvic pain after uterine instrumentation? Assess tubal patency.
submission.pre_read_summary: 32F with 6 months of amenorrhea, progressively diminished menstrual flow and worsening dysmenorrhea after D&C for missed abortion ~1 year ago; prior septic abortion and cervical LEEP/conization. Pregnancy test negative; FSH, LH, prolactin and TSH normal. HSG documentation reports a uterine-cavity filling defect and scant contrast passage into the proximal fallopian tubes. Postprocedural intrauterine synechiae are favored; prior LEEP raises possibility of cervical stenosis. Currently breastfeeding, which may also contribute to amenorrhea.
must_include_findings: Location, extent and configuration of uterine-cavity filling defect(s), especially irregular adhesions, cavity distortion or partial obliteration
Degree of cervical canal narrowing and adequacy of contrast filling of the uterine cavity
Opacification of each fallopian tube, site of any obstruction and presence or absence of bilateral free peritoneal spill
Whether apparent proximal tubal nonfilling could reflect limited injection, uterine adhesions or tubal spasm rather than fixed tubal obstruction

differential.diagnosis: Intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) following dilation and curettage
Proximal tubal obstruction or adhesions related to prior pelvic infection
Endometrial polyp or submucosal leiomyoma causing intracavitary filling defect

submission.clinical_question: Does carotid duplex demonstrate hemodynamically significant left internal carotid artery stenosis as the source of a left-hemispheric TIA, and is there additional bilateral carotid disease relevant to stroke prevention or revascularization?
submission.pre_read_summary: 67–68M with sudden right-arm weakness and speech difficulty resolving completely within 1 hour, consistent with left-hemispheric TIA. Left carotid bruit; history of bilateral cerebrovascular disease, PAD, CAD/PCI, repaired AAA, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and prior heavy smoking. On aspirin and atorvastatin. Encounter documentation reports carotid Doppler showing approximately 75% left ICA stenosis; assess severity and contralateral disease.
must_include_findings: Bilateral common carotid, bulb, and internal carotid plaque distribution and morphology, including ulceration if visible
Peak systolic and end-diastolic velocities and ICA/CCA ratios bilaterally; estimated percent left ICA stenosis (reported approximately 75%) and right ICA stenosis
Patency versus near-occlusion or complete occlusion of either internal carotid artery
Bilateral vertebral artery flow direction and patency; significant subclavian disease if assessed

differential.diagnosis: Symptomatic atherosclerotic left internal carotid artery stenosis

submission.clinical_question: What is the nature of the palpable left breast mass, and are there imaging features suspicious for breast malignancy requiring biopsy?
submission.pre_read_summary: 29-year-old woman with a self-detected, firm, nontender 2.4-cm mass in the left upper outer breast, without skin changes or nipple retraction. Encounter documentation describes a suspicious irregular mammographic lesion; core needle biopsy is pending. Strong family history of early-onset/bilateral breast cancer (sister diagnosed at 35; mother reportedly diagnosed at 45) and ovarian cancer (maternal grandmother). Childhood Wilms tumor treated with nephrectomy and abdominopelvic radiation; Crohn disease treated with adalimumab. Prior radiation is documented as abdominopelvic, not chest irradiation.
must_include_findings: Site, size, and mammographic morphology/margins of the lesion corresponding to the palpable left upper outer breast mass
Targeted ultrasound correlation and whether the lesion is solid or cystic, if performed
Associated suspicious calcifications or architectural distortion
Left axillary lymph nodes and any additional ipsilateral or contralateral suspicious findings
Final BI-RADS assessment and recommendation for image-guided core biopsy

differential.diagnosis: Breast carcinoma, including invasive ductal carcinoma

submission.clinical_question: Does high-speed blunt trauma with an unstable pelvis and shock reflect a pelvic fracture with active pelvic/retroperitoneal hemorrhage, and are there associated abdominal or pelvic organ injuries?
submission.pre_read_summary: 22M after high-speed MVC with severe pelvic pain, pelvic instability, lower abdominal/perineal ecchymosis, BP 90/60, HR 120, and hemoglobin 9 g/dL (prior 14). FAST negative for intraperitoneal fluid. CT abdomen/pelvis is requested to characterize pelvic injury and identify occult hemorrhage or visceral injury; negative FAST does not exclude retroperitoneal bleeding.
must_include_findings: Pelvic ring and acetabular fractures, including displacement and sacroiliac or pubic symphyseal diastasis
Pelvic and retroperitoneal hematoma, its extent, and any active contrast extravasation or arterial injury
Hemoperitoneum and solid-organ or bowel/mesenteric injury
Bladder injury or perivesical hemorrhage; correlate perineal ecchymosis with possible urethral injury, which may require dedicated evaluation

differential.diagnosis: Pelvic ring fracture with associated retroperitoneal hemorrhage
Traumatic injury of pelvic blood vessels with active hemorrhage

submission.clinical_question: Does mitral valve prolapse account for the apical click and late systolic murmur, and what is the severity and hemodynamic impact of associated mitral regurgitation?
submission.pre_read_summary: 37-year-old woman with childhood heart murmur and maternal mitral valve prolapse, now with 6 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and palpitations. Examination reveals a midsystolic click and late systolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla; ECG shows atrial fibrillation (rate 92). Available transthoracic echo description reports systolic mitral leaflet prolapse, significant mitral regurgitation, and left atrial enlargement. No reported chest pain, syncope, or edema.
must_include_findings: Mitral leaflet systolic displacement/prolapse, involved leaflet(s), leaflet morphology, and any flail segment or chordal rupture
Mitral regurgitation mechanism, jet direction, and quantitative severity if feasible
Left atrial and left ventricular size and left ventricular systolic function
Estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure and right ventricular size/function
Any additional valvular abnormalities

differential.diagnosis: Mitral valve prolapse with mitral regurgitation
Primary (degenerative) mitral regurgitation due to flail leaflet or chordal rupture
Functional mitral regurgitation associated with atrial or ventricular remodeling
Atrial fibrillation associated with left atrial enlargement and mitral regurgitation
Pulmonary hypertension secondary to left-sided valvular disease

submission.clinical_question: Is there an acute intracranial abnormality or structural brain lesion accounting for altered behavior and psychosis?
submission.pre_read_summary: Young adult man with schizophrenia and progressive social withdrawal and paranoid delusions since 2019, presenting with two weeks of worsening erratic behavior, auditory hallucinations, and paranoia. No medications; vital signs, CBC, CMP, and urine toxicology are unremarkable. Head CT is requested to exclude an intracranial cause of altered mental status; the available chart describes the CT as normal.
must_include_findings: Acute intracranial hemorrhage or extra-axial collection
Intracranial mass, mass effect, or midline shift
Acute territorial infarction or other focal parenchymal abnormality
Ventricular size and hydrocephalus

differential.diagnosis: Substance-induced psychotic disorder, less likely with negative toxicology

submission.clinical_question: What is the sonographic correlate of the palpable right upper outer breast mass, and is it a simple cyst or a solid/suspicious lesion requiring further evaluation?
submission.pre_read_summary: 42-year-old woman with a stable, painless palpable right upper outer breast mass for one month. Exam: smooth, mobile mass without skin or nipple changes, discharge, or axillary adenopathy. History of fibrocystic changes and prior benign right breast fibroadenoma excision (2019); mammogram 18 months ago reportedly normal. Encounter documentation describes a 2-cm simple cyst on ultrasound, with complete resolution after aspiration of nonbloody, straw-colored fluid.
must_include_findings: Targeted ultrasound correlation with the palpable right upper outer breast lump, including location and dimensions
Cystic versus solid composition; if cystic, assess anechoic contents, thin wall, posterior acoustic enhancement, septations or mural solid components, and Doppler vascularity
Any suspicious adjacent breast lesion or abnormal right axillary lymph nodes
If aspiration is performed, document complete or incomplete sonographic resolution and any residual solid component
BI-RADS assessment and recommendation for further imaging or biopsy if findings are not definitively benign

differential.diagnosis: Simple breast cyst associated with fibrocystic change

submission.clinical_question: Is there a mammographic abnormality, particularly a suspicious mass or calcifications, underlying focal noncyclic left upper-outer breast pain?
submission.pre_read_summary: Woman in her 40s with 3 months of sharp, focal, noncyclic left upper-outer quadrant breast pain. No palpable mass, nipple discharge, skin change, retraction, or axillary adenopathy on examination. Prior mammogram approximately 18 months ago was normal; no family history of breast cancer. Medication list includes tamoxifen, but its indication is not documented.
must_include_findings: At the symptomatic left upper-outer quadrant, presence or absence of a mass, focal asymmetry, or architectural distortion
Suspicious microcalcifications in either breast
Skin or nipple changes and visible axillary adenopathy
Comparison with prior mammogram and final BI-RADS assessment; recommend targeted ultrasound if mammography does not explain persistent focal pain

differential.diagnosis: Focal noncyclic mastalgia without imaging abnormality

submission.clinical_question: Does renal artery stenosis, particularly right-sided stenosis due to fibromuscular dysplasia, explain this young patient's new-onset marked hypertension and right abdominal bruit?
submission.pre_read_summary: 33-year-old woman with newly diagnosed hypertension (168/100 mmHg bilaterally), several weeks of headache and fatigue, and a right periumbilical abdominal bruit. Normal renal function and electrolytes; BMI 23, nonsmoker. Mother developed hypertension at 32; paternal uncle had renal artery stenosis. Abdominal CTA requested to evaluate renovascular hypertension, particularly fibromuscular dysplasia.
must_include_findings: Presence, location, severity, and laterality of renal artery stenosis, especially the right renal artery
Beaded appearance or alternating stenosis and dilatation of the mid-to-distal renal arteries suggesting fibromuscular dysplasia
Ostial or proximal renal artery plaque suggesting atherosclerotic stenosis
Accessory renal arteries, renal artery aneurysm or dissection, and renal size/asymmetry or perfusion changes

differential.diagnosis: Renal artery stenosis from another cause, including atherosclerosis

submission.clinical_question: Does head CT show a focal intracranial lesion, hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, or mass effect explaining progressive encephalopathy and right-sided weakness in a patient with advanced AIDS?
submission.pre_read_summary: 44F with advanced HIV/AIDS (most recent CD4 70 cells/mm³), on ART and TMP-SMX for PJP prophylaxis, with prior CMV disease. One week of worsening headache and confusion, now nonverbal and lethargic; examination shows disorientation and mild right-sided weakness. Evaluate urgently for opportunistic CNS infection or intracranial mass, including complications that would affect safety of lumbar puncture.
must_include_findings: Presence, number, distribution, and size of focal parenchymal lesions, especially basal ganglia or corticomedullary lesions; surrounding edema and mass effect
Intracranial hemorrhage or acute territorial infarction
Midline shift, ventricular compression, hydrocephalus, or herniation
Meningeal abnormalities or other evidence of CNS infection, recognizing limited sensitivity of noncontrast CT

submission.clinical_question: What is the nature of the palpable right adnexal mass in this premenarchal adolescent, particularly is it an ovarian dermoid (mature cystic teratoma), and is there evidence of torsion or concerning malignant features?
submission.pre_read_summary: 12-year-old premenarchal girl with 4 days of intermittent lower abdominal discomfort and fullness. Examination finds a firm, nontender right adnexal mass; abdomen is soft and nontender. β-hCG and inflammatory markers are normal. Pelvic ultrasound documentation describes an approximately 8-cm right ovarian mass with mixed solid/cystic components and calcifications, without ascites or reported metastatic disease. Findings strongly suggest mature cystic teratoma; characterize the lesion and assess ovarian vascularity given pain and mass size.
must_include_findings: Right ovarian mass size, origin, and solid/cystic composition; echogenic fat or calcifications and posterior shadowing suggestive of dermoid
Right ovarian and adnexal Doppler flow, ovarian enlargement or edema, twisted pedicle, and free fluid as signs of torsion (preserved flow does not exclude torsion)
Presence of suspicious vascular solid nodules, irregularity, or other malignant features
Contralateral ovary and any additional adnexal lesions
Pelvic free fluid or ascites

differential.diagnosis: Mature cystic teratoma of right ovary
Ovarian torsion associated with adnexal mass
Other ovarian germ-cell tumor, including immature teratoma

submission.clinical_question: Is a left renal mass, particularly renal cell carcinoma, the source of gross hematuria and left flank pain, and is there evidence of collecting-system obstruction or renal vein involvement?
submission.pre_read_summary: 57F with 3 days of gross hematuria, dull left flank pain and left CVA tenderness, plus unintentional 10-kg weight loss over 2 months. Former smoker (30 pack-years). Hematocrit 55% (previously 39.8%), raising concern for paraneoplastic erythrocytosis. Encounter documentation describes a heterogeneous left renal mass on ultrasound; characterize and assess for malignancy. Intermittent headaches and blurred vision may relate to erythrocytosis.
must_include_findings: Left renal mass: location, dimensions, solid versus cystic composition, heterogeneity, vascularity and any necrotic or hemorrhagic components
Renal collecting system: hydronephrosis, calculi and intraluminal mass or clot
Visible renal vein or IVC involvement/tumor thrombus, if assessable
Contralateral kidney and any additional renal lesions

differential.diagnosis: Renal cell carcinoma, with possible erythropoietin-mediated secondary erythrocytosis
Upper tract urothelial carcinoma of the left renal pelvis

submission.clinical_question: Is there hematocolpos or hematometrocolpos due to an imperforate hymen or other vaginal outflow obstruction, and is there associated urinary tract obstruction?
submission.pre_read_summary: Adolescent with primary amenorrhea and prior cyclic pelvic pain, now with 6 hours of severe crampy suprapubic pain, lower abdominal distention, and difficulty defecating. Examination shows a bulging bluish membrane at the vaginal introitus with no visible opening, strongly suggesting imperforate hymen and retained menstrual blood. Prior documentation of androgen insensitivity/5-alpha-reductase deficiency and absent uterus conflicts with the current examination and reported sonographic visualization of a normal uterus; clarify pelvic anatomy on this study.
must_include_findings: Vaginal distention and character of its contents, including echogenic blood products or fluid–fluid levels consistent with hematocolpos
Uterine presence and anatomy; endometrial cavity distention or hematometra
Level of vaginal outflow obstruction and any visible obstructing membrane or septum
Ovaries/adnexa, including masses or torsion findings if visualized
Bladder distention, hydronephrosis or other renal abnormalities from mass effect

differential.diagnosis: Hematometra due to genital outflow obstruction

submission.clinical_question: Has the prior right lower lung abscess resolved, and does the persistent rounded opacity represent residual postinfectious change or an underlying pulmonary mass?
submission.pre_read_summary: 65-year-old man with post-stroke oropharyngeal dysphagia and prior aspiration-related right lower lung abscess, initially cavitary with an air–fluid level. He completed prolonged clindamycin approximately one year ago and is now asymptomatic, with negative sputum cultures and inflammatory markers. Follow-up chest radiograph reportedly shows a persistent rounded opacity in the same region; compare with prior imaging and assess for a nonresolving lesion.
must_include_findings: Size, location, and interval change of the right lower lung rounded opacity compared with prior imaging
Whether residual cavitation or an air–fluid level persists
Any surrounding consolidation or new infiltrates suggesting active infection or recurrent aspiration
Whether the opacity has features concerning for an underlying mass; recommend chest CT if persistent or indeterminate

differential.diagnosis: Residual postinfectious scarring or organizing pneumonia
Primary pulmonary malignancy presenting as a persistent mass or postobstructive infection

submission.clinical_question: Does the chest radiograph show pneumonia or pulmonary edema to explain new cough and dyspnea, versus medication-related cough after starting lisinopril?
submission.pre_read_summary: 64M with CAD/prior MI, hypertension, diabetes, active smoking (40 pack-years), and laryngeal cancer presents with cough and dyspnea beginning about 2 weeks after starting lisinopril. Bibasilar crackles, SpO₂ 94% on room air; afebrile by history, no chest pain or leg swelling. WBC 7 and BNP 80 pg/mL. Assess for cardiopulmonary cause of symptoms; lisinopril-associated cough is also suspected.
must_include_findings: Focal airspace opacity or infiltrate suggesting pneumonia
Pulmonary vascular congestion or interstitial/alveolar edema
Cardiac silhouette size
Pleural effusion or pneumothorax
Visible pulmonary mass or suspicious nodule given smoking and cancer history

differential.diagnosis: Pulmonary vascular congestion or mild cardiogenic pulmonary edema

submission.clinical_question: Does obstetric ultrasound confirm and quantify polyhydramnios, and is there an identifiable fetal, placental, or maternal-associated cause?
submission.pre_read_summary: 28-year-old primigravida presenting with increasing abdominal distension and fundal height greater than expected for gestational age. Prenatal history includes retained copper IUD and placenta previa; she denies contractions, fluid leakage, and vaginal bleeding. Current ultrasound note describes increased amniotic fluid index/excess fluid with normal Dopplers; no numerical AFI or gestational age for this visit is documented. Assess fluid volume and fetal anatomy, growth, and well-being, as well as placental location and IUD position. Paternal family history includes VACTERL-associated congenital anomalies; diabetes screening status is unavailable.
must_include_findings: Numeric amniotic fluid index and/or deepest vertical pocket, with polyhydramnios severity
Fetal number, presentation, growth/estimated fetal weight, and cardiac activity
Targeted fetal anatomy, especially stomach visibility and gastrointestinal obstruction signs, facial cleft, CNS anomalies, and other congenital anomalies
Placental location relative to internal cervical os and any signs of placental abnormality
Location of retained IUD relative to gestational sac, placenta, and cervix if visible
Fetal Doppler assessment and evidence of hydrops or anemia, if assessed

differential.diagnosis: Fetal congenital anomaly, including gastrointestinal obstruction or impaired swallowing

submission.clinical_question: Is there pneumonia or another acute intrathoracic process causing hypoxia and altered mental status in a patient with suspected sepsis?
submission.pre_read_summary: 65M with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma, severe COPD on 2 L home oxygen, and CKD presents with several days of worsening productive cough, acute confusion, and poor intake. Hypothermic (35.5°C), hypotensive (84/52), tachycardic (122), tachypneic (26), and SpO₂ 90% on room air; decreased right basilar breath sounds and bibasilar crackles. WBC 23,000, lactate 4.5, creatinine 2.1. Available chest radiograph description notes large right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, concerning for pneumonia with septic shock.
must_include_findings: Right lower lobe consolidation and air bronchograms; extent and other areas of airspace opacity
Pleural effusion or empyema and pneumothorax
Known lung mass or evidence of airway obstruction/postobstructive change, if visible
Pulmonary edema or other acute cardiopulmonary abnormality

differential.diagnosis: Right lower lobe bacterial pneumonia with sepsis
Postobstructive pneumonia related to lung adenocarcinoma
Right lower lobe atelectasis from bronchial obstruction

submission.clinical_question: What is the cause of new ascites and bilateral adnexal masses—primary ovarian malignancy with peritoneal carcinomatosis versus metastatic pancreatic carcinoma? Assess extent of intra-abdominal disease.
submission.pre_read_summary: Woman with pancreatic carcinoma diagnosed in 2024, chronic pancreatitis and diabetes presents with 3 months of progressive abdominal enlargement, early satiety, fatigue and 6-kg unintentional weight loss. Examination shows fluid wave and bilateral adnexal fullness without signs of chronic liver disease. CT abdomen/pelvis is documented as showing large-volume ascites, multiple solid pelvic masses and diffuse omental thickening, concerning for peritoneal malignancy. Family history includes ovarian and breast cancer. IMPORTANT: documented anaphylaxis to iodinated contrast.
must_include_findings: Ascites volume and any loculation
Size, laterality and morphology of ovarian/adnexal or other pelvic masses; relationship to uterus
Omental thickening/caking and peritoneal implants, including sites and extent
Pancreatic primary lesion or local recurrence and other possible primary tumor
Hepatic lesions, lymphadenopathy and other metastatic disease
Bowel involvement or obstruction and hydronephrosis
Document iodinated contrast anaphylaxis before any contrast administration

differential.diagnosis: Primary epithelial ovarian carcinoma with peritoneal carcinomatosis
Peritoneal metastases from known pancreatic carcinoma, with ovarian metastases
Ascites from portal hypertension or other nonmalignant etiology, less likely given solid masses and omental thickening

submission.clinical_question: Does the left leg have deep venous thrombosis, particularly involving the popliteal vein, and what is its extent?
submission.pre_read_summary: 54-year-old woman with 3 days of progressive left calf pain and swelling after prolonged car travel 2 weeks ago. Left calf is warm, erythematous, tender, and 3 cm larger than the right, with pitting edema from ankle to mid-calf. No trauma; father had DVT. History includes rheumatoid arthritis treated with chronic prednisone, diabetes, and hypertension. Encounter documentation describes a noncompressible left popliteal vein, consistent with DVT.
must_include_findings: Compressibility and intraluminal thrombus of the left popliteal vein
Extent of thrombus into femoral and calf deep veins, including whether occlusive or nonocclusive
Color and spectral Doppler flow in the evaluated deep veins
Any alternative explanation for calf swelling, such as a popliteal cyst or soft-tissue fluid collection

differential.diagnosis: Superficial thrombophlebitis of left lower extremity

submission.clinical_question: Is there a new or recurrent left humeral shaft fracture, including a fracture adjacent to prior fixation hardware, after the ladder fall, and is hardware intact and alignment preserved?
submission.pre_read_summary: 33-year-old man fell from a ladder onto his left arm, with immediate sharp mid-upper-arm pain, swelling, bruising, and deformity. Prior left humeral shaft fracture treated with ORIF and history of radial nerve injury. Currently unable to extend the left wrist or fingers, with decreased sensation over the dorsal hand/thumb, concerning for radial nerve dysfunction. Skin intact; radial and ulnar pulses symmetric.
must_include_findings: Presence and location of any acute left humeral fracture, including relationship to the prior fracture and fixation hardware
Fracture morphology, displacement, angulation, and alignment
Integrity of fixation hardware, including loosening or breakage
Elbow and shoulder alignment if included in the radiographs
Associated soft-tissue swelling

differential.diagnosis: Acute or recurrent left humeral shaft fracture with radial nerve palsy
Periprosthetic fracture adjacent to left humeral fixation hardware
Failure or loosening of left humeral fixation hardware
Left upper-arm contusion with radial nerve neuropraxia, without new fracture

submission.clinical_question: Are there suspicious pulmonary nodules or other evidence of lung cancer on screening chest CT in this smoker?
submission.pre_read_summary: 58-year-old man with tobacco use and COPD requests lung cancer screening; father died of lung cancer at age 62. He is asymptomatic, examination is unremarkable, and recent chest radiograph showed no acute findings. Smoking pack-years and current versus former status are not documented; confirm eligibility for low-dose screening CT.
must_include_findings: Presence, size, location, attenuation (solid versus subsolid), and morphology of any pulmonary nodules or masses; comparison with prior imaging if available
Suspicious associated findings, including hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy and pleural abnormalities
Emphysema or other smoking-related lung changes
Lung-RADS category and recommended follow-up if performed as low-dose screening CT

submission.clinical_question: Does CT show acute pancreatitis or complications of recurrent pancreatitis in the setting of severe hypertriglyceridemia, and is there an alternative cause of upper abdominal pain?
submission.pre_read_summary: 23-year-old man with recurrent severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea/vomiting, and epigastric tenderness. Triglycerides 2,000 mg/dL, amylase 2,000 U/L, lipase 1,800 U/L, strongly supporting acute hypertriglyceridemia-associated pancreatitis. Prior similar episodes required hospitalization. Reported imaging shows no gallstones or biliary obstruction; alcohol use is modest (2–3 drinks/week).
must_include_findings: Pancreatic enlargement and peripancreatic edema or fat stranding; distribution and severity of inflammation
Pancreatic parenchymal enhancement and any areas of necrosis, if IV contrast administered
Acute peripancreatic fluid collections, pseudocyst or walled-off necrosis, particularly given recurrent episodes
Pancreatic duct caliber and evidence of chronic pancreatitis, including calcifications
Biliary duct dilation, gallstones if visible, or other evidence of biliary obstruction
Complications including splenic/portal vein thrombosis, hemorrhage, ascites, or adjacent bowel involvement
Alternative acute abdominal pathology if pancreatic findings do not account for symptoms

differential.diagnosis: Acute pancreatitis due to severe hypertriglyceridemia
Acute recurrent pancreatitis with pancreatic fluid collection or pseudocyst
Acute biliary pancreatitis (less likely given reported absence of gallstones or obstruction)

submission.clinical_question: In a patient with COPD and acute worsening dyspnea, productive cough, fever, and hypoxemia, is there radiographic pneumonia or another acute cardiopulmonary process?
submission.pre_read_summary: 67-year-old man with moderate–severe COPD and ongoing smoking (40 pack-years) presents with 3 days of worsening dyspnea, green sputum, and low-grade fever. SpO2 89% on room air, RR 22, HR 102; diffuse wheezing and prolonged expiration. Room-air ABG: pH 7.36, PaCO2 50, PaO2 60 mmHg. Chest radiograph is described in the encounter as hyperinflated without consolidation, favoring an acute COPD exacerbation without radiographically apparent pneumonia.
must_include_findings: Presence or absence and location of focal airspace consolidation or infiltrate
Hyperinflation/emphysematous change
Pleural effusion or pneumothorax
Other acute cardiopulmonary abnormality, including pulmonary edema

differential.diagnosis: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

submission.clinical_question: What is the cause of headache and bilateral papilledema—are there intracranial mass, hydrocephalus, venous sinus thrombosis, or imaging signs of intracranial hypertension consistent with idiopathic intracranial hypertension?
submission.pre_read_summary: 35-year-old woman with obesity (BMI 35) and 2 months of daily morning-predominant headaches, transient visual obscurations, and pulse-synchronous tinnitus. Examination shows bilateral papilledema with preserved acuity and visual fields; BP 130/85. LP opening pressure documented at 280 mm H2O. Brain MRI with and without contrast is documented as normal. Clinical picture strongly favors idiopathic intracranial hypertension after exclusion of structural and venous causes.
must_include_findings: Intracranial mass, abnormal enhancement, or other space-occupying lesion
Hydrocephalus or other cause of CSF outflow obstruction
Dural venous sinus thrombosis or stenosis; recommend MR venography if not adequately assessed by this examination
Signs of raised intracranial pressure, including partially empty sella, posterior globe flattening, optic nerve sheath distention/tortuosity, or optic disc protrusion

submission.clinical_question: Does the chest radiograph show pneumonia or another acute pulmonary process accounting for fever in this patient with severe mucocutaneous illness?
submission.pre_read_summary: Adult man admitted to ICU with fever and tachycardia after a recent upper respiratory illness and short course of an unspecified oral medication. He has extensive bullous skin sloughing with oral, ocular, and genital erosions, concerning for Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis; mild leukopenia and elevated liver enzymes. Chest radiograph is documented as unremarkable. Evaluate for pneumonia or other pulmonary involvement/infection.
must_include_findings: Presence or absence of focal airspace consolidation or multifocal infiltrates
Presence or absence of pleural effusion and pneumothorax
Presence or absence of diffuse interstitial or alveolar opacities suggesting pulmonary involvement or edema

differential.diagnosis: Pulmonary involvement of Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis

submission.clinical_question: Following traumatic right-hand crush injury and fasciotomy, is there a residual hematoma, soft-tissue injury, or vascular compromise? Confirm the intended imaging site, as the documented acute ischemic findings concern the left lower leg.
submission.pre_read_summary: 32M after motorcycle accident with prolonged extrication. The chart documents right-hand crush injury with fasciotomy for compartment syndrome, but provides no current hand examination or specific hand symptoms. The active ED assessment instead describes severe left lower-leg pain, swelling, pallor, weak distal pulses, sensory and motor deficit; prior arterial Doppler reportedly showed acute occlusion, followed by embolectomy. CK 2500 U/L and myoglobin 150 ng/mL. The upper-extremity ultrasound indication is 'hand trauma'; laterality/site and intended clinical question should be clarified.
must_include_findings: Confirm laterality and target of ultrasound before interpretation (record identifies right-hand crush injury but current vascular symptoms are left-leg).
If examining the hand, characterize any focal fluid collection or hematoma, muscle edema, and soft-tissue disruption.
If Doppler is performed, document patency and flow of accessible radial and ulnar arteries and palmar vessels, including any occlusion or pseudoaneurysm.
Document any findings suspicious for persistent or recurrent compartment-related swelling; ultrasound cannot exclude compartment syndrome.

differential.diagnosis: Traumatic compartment syndrome of right upper extremity
Injury of blood vessel of right upper extremity

submission.clinical_question: Does the chest radiograph show pulmonary vascular congestion or edema from recurrent decompensated heart failure as the cause of dyspnea?
submission.pre_read_summary: Man with HFrEF (LVEF 30% in January 2022), hypertension, ASCVD, and polycythemia vera presenting with worsening three-pillow orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea over weeks despite home furosemide. Exam shows JVD, S3, bibasilar crackles, and mild bilateral ankle edema. Prior chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion; current chart describes prominent pulmonary vessels and mild bibasilar hazy opacities. No fever or recent illness reported.
must_include_findings: Cardiac silhouette size and comparison with prior cardiomegaly
Pulmonary vascular congestion and interstitial or alveolar edema, including bibasilar hazy opacities
Pleural effusions
Focal airspace consolidation or other alternative acute pulmonary process

differential.diagnosis: Acute on chronic systolic heart failure with cardiogenic pulmonary edema

submission.clinical_question: Is there an obstructing distal gastric/pyloric malignancy causing impaired gastric emptying, and is there regional or distant spread?
submission.pre_read_summary: Older man with months of progressive postprandial epigastric pain, early satiety, nausea, reduced intake and 15-lb unintentional weight loss. Mild iron-deficiency anemia and epigastric tenderness; normal liver enzymes. Prior upper abdominal imaging suggests delayed gastric emptying with distal gastric narrowing, and pyloric biopsy shows malignancy. History includes longstanding poorly controlled diabetes and CKD.
must_include_findings: Location, size, extent, and enhancement of any distal gastric/pyloric wall thickening or mass
Degree of gastric distention, pyloric narrowing, and gastric outlet obstruction
Invasion of adjacent structures and perigastric fat
Regional and distant lymphadenopathy
Hepatic, peritoneal/omental, and other abdominopelvic metastases or ascites
Other potential causes of epigastric pain or gastric outlet obstruction

differential.diagnosis: Pyloric gastric adenocarcinoma with gastric outlet obstruction

submission.clinical_question: Is an infected obstructing left staghorn calculus present, with hydronephrosis or complications of pyelonephritis that could explain persistent fever and flank pain despite antibiotics?
submission.pre_read_summary: 52F with recurrent nephrolithiasis and UTIs, presenting with fever, hematuria, and left flank pain persisting despite antibiotics. Urinalysis: pH 7.6, pyuria, hematuria, and coffin-lid crystals, suggesting infection-associated struvite stone; available imaging documentation describes a large left renal pelvic staghorn calculus. Chart inconsistently documents prior left nephrectomy versus nephrectomy during this episode; verify operative timing/anatomy. Prior contrast-dye anaphylaxis.
must_include_findings: Presence, size, and extent of left renal pelvic staghorn calculus and any additional urinary tract calculi
Left renal anatomy and confirmation of whether nephrectomy has occurred
Hydronephrosis or urinary obstruction and renal parenchymal destruction
Perinephric inflammation, renal or perinephric abscess, and emphysematous infection
Condition of the contralateral kidney and collecting system

submission.clinical_question: Has the previously identified 6 mm noncalcified right lower lobe pulmonary nodule grown or developed suspicious features suggesting primary lung malignancy, and are there additional nodules?
submission.pre_read_summary: 45-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history and COPD, asymptomatic at pulmonology follow-up. Prior screening low-dose chest CT identified a solitary 6 mm noncalcified right lower lobe nodule. Follow-up chest CT is requested to assess interval stability and malignancy risk; paternal uncle had lung cancer.
must_include_findings: Current size and location of the right lower lobe nodule compared with prior CT, including interval growth or resolution
Nodule attenuation, margins, and suspicious features such as spiculation or a new solid component
Any additional pulmonary nodules or masses
Mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy

differential.diagnosis: Benign pulmonary nodule, including postinflammatory or granulomatous nodule

submission.clinical_question: Does brain MRI show structural lesions causing infantile spasms, particularly tuberous sclerosis complex–associated cortical tubers or subependymal lesions, and is there an obstructing subependymal giant cell astrocytoma or progression of known hydrocephalus?
submission.pre_read_summary: Infant boy with frequent daily staring spells/spasms for two months, developmental delay and EEG hypsarrhythmia; taking vigabatrin. Hypopigmented truncal macules, a raised back plaque, cardiac rhabdomyoma, and paternal history of tuberous sclerosis strongly suggest TSC. The order-encounter MRI documentation describes cortical tubers and subependymal nodules. Prior MRI showed Dandy–Walker-spectrum malformation (fourth-ventricular cystic dilatation, vermian hypoplasia, enlarged posterior fossa); prior examination noted macrocephaly, bulging fontanelle, vomiting, and hypotonia, concerning for hydrocephalus.
must_include_findings: Cortical and subcortical tubers, including location, burden, and any associated cortical dysplasia or white-matter radial migration lines
Subependymal nodules, including whether calcified and whether any lesion near the foramen of Monro enlarges or enhances, suggesting subependymal giant cell astrocytoma
Lateral and third ventricular size, ventricular outflow obstruction, hydrocephalus, and transependymal CSF flow
Fourth-ventricular cystic dilation, cerebellar vermian hypoplasia, enlarged posterior fossa, and any interval change in the Dandy–Walker-spectrum malformation
Other structural epileptogenic lesions or malformations of cortical development

differential.diagnosis: Tuberous sclerosis complex with cortical tubers and subependymal nodules
Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Other malformation of cortical development or focal cortical dysplasia

submission.clinical_question: Does the endoscopic distribution and appearance of colitis support active left-sided ulcerative colitis rather than Crohn colitis or infectious colitis, and are inflammatory pseudopolyps present?
submission.pre_read_summary: Woman with 6 months of bloody diarrhea (up to six stools daily, including nocturnal stools), abdominal pain, weight loss, and mild LLQ tenderness. Hgb 10.2 g/dL, ESR 45 mm/hr, CRP 25 mg/L, albumin 3.2 g/dL; stool cultures and C. difficile assay negative. Taking mesalamine; chart lists Crohn disease, reportedly initially classified as ulcerative colitis. Colonoscopy describes continuous ulcerated inflammation from rectum to splenic flexure with pseudopolyps; biopsies show chronic inflammation confined to mucosa/submucosa. Pattern favors active left-sided ulcerative colitis.
must_include_findings: Continuity and proximal extent of inflammation from rectum through splenic flexure; whether there are skip lesions or ileal involvement
Severity of mucosal erythema, friability and ulceration, including any spontaneous bleeding
Presence, distribution and appearance of inflammatory pseudopolyps; identify any suspicious focal mass or lesion
Evidence of stricture, deep ulceration, fistula or other features suggesting Crohn disease

submission.clinical_question: Is there significant postpartum bladder distention/urinary retention, and is there a pelvic structural or obstetric cause of impaired voiding?
submission.pre_read_summary: Postpartum patient 8 hours after spontaneous vaginal delivery with epidural analgesia and episiotomy repair, unable to void despite urgency, with suprapubic fullness, discomfort and small-volume leakage on attempted voiding. Bladder scan shows 600 mL residual. Assess bladder volume and pelvic causes of acute postpartum urinary retention; leakage may represent overflow.
must_include_findings: Bladder distention and measured pre- and postvoid bladder volumes/residual, if voiding is possible
Bladder wall appearance and any intravesical clot or debris
Any pelvic or periurethral hematoma or mass causing bladder outlet compression
Uterine position and postpartum uterine or pelvic abnormalities that could affect bladder emptying
Upper urinary tract dilatation if kidneys are included in the examination

differential.diagnosis: Acute postpartum urinary retention due to transient detrusor dysfunction after epidural analgesia and vaginal delivery
Postpartum bladder outlet obstruction due to perineal swelling or pelvic hematoma
Overflow urinary incontinence secondary to bladder overdistention

submission.clinical_question: Does the chest radiograph show pulmonary edema consistent with high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), and is there an alternative cause of hypoxemic dyspnea?
submission.pre_read_summary: 32-year-old woman with progressive dyspnea and dry cough after rapid ascent to 12,000 feet over two days. SpO₂ 86% on room air, PaO₂ 55 mmHg, tachypnea and bibasilar crackles; afebrile with low procalcitonin and no reported infectious contacts. Family history of HAPE susceptibility. The encounter documents bilateral alveolar infiltrates on chest radiograph. Evaluate for noncardiogenic pulmonary edema due to altitude exposure versus infection or cardiogenic edema.
must_include_findings: Distribution and extent of bilateral airspace/alveolar opacities, including any patchy or asymmetric edema pattern
Cardiac silhouette size and signs of pulmonary venous congestion to distinguish cardiogenic edema
Pleural effusions or pneumothorax
Focal consolidation suggesting pneumonia

differential.diagnosis: Acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema from another cause

submission.clinical_question: Is an obstructing right ureteral calculus causing renal colic, and what is its location and degree of upstream obstruction?
submission.pre_read_summary: 46M with recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis presents with 2 days of severe intermittent right flank pain radiating to the groin, nausea/vomiting, and right CVA tenderness. Afebrile; urinalysis shows hematuria without pyuria or bacteriuria. Encounter documentation reports a 5 mm right ureteral calculus on noncontrast CT; assess location and obstruction.
must_include_findings: Size and precise location of the reported 5 mm right ureteral calculus
Right hydronephrosis or hydroureter and severity; perinephric or periureteral stranding
Additional renal or ureteral calculi, including contralateral stones
Other acute abdominal or pelvic pathology if present

submission.clinical_question: Does the uterine cavity contain a hydatidiform mole (complete versus partial), and is there a viable intrauterine pregnancy or another cause of first-trimester bleeding?
submission.pre_read_summary: 32-year-old at approximately 12 weeks by LMP with two weeks of worsening vaginal bleeding. β-hCG 450,000 mIU/mL, suppressed TSH and elevated free T4 with tachycardia, palpitations and heat intolerance, raising strong concern for gestational trophoblastic disease with hCG-mediated hyperthyroidism. Available pelvic ultrasound description notes an enlarged uterus containing a heterogeneous multicystic intracavitary mass. History includes recurrent pregnancy loss, submucosal fibroid status post myomectomy, SLE/antiphospholipid syndrome and Factor V Leiden; medication list includes warfarin and aspirin.
must_include_findings: Size and morphology of the heterogeneous multicystic intrauterine mass and characteristic molar vesicles
Presence or absence of a gestational sac, embryo or fetus, and fetal cardiac activity; assess for coexisting normal gestation
Endometrial/myometrial interface and any evidence of myometrial invasion or marked vascularity on Doppler
Adnexal evaluation for bilateral theca lutein cysts and ectopic pregnancy
Any intrauterine or pelvic hemorrhage or free fluid

differential.diagnosis: Failed intrauterine pregnancy with retained products of conception
Submucosal uterine leiomyoma with pregnancy-associated bleeding

submission.clinical_question: Does this patient with suspected sleep-disordered breathing have sonographic evidence of pulmonary hypertension and right-heart strain/cor pulmonale?
submission.pre_read_summary: 53M with BMI 35, enlarged neck, daytime somnolence and morning headaches, referred for suspected sleep apnea. Awake room-air PaCO2 55 mmHg, PaO2 68 mmHg, HCO3 32 mEq/L indicate chronic hypercapnic hypoxemia, favoring obesity hypoventilation syndrome with coexisting obstructive sleep apnea. Hgb 18.5/Hct 55% suggest secondary erythrocytosis; leg edema and a documented echocardiogram showing RV hypertrophy raise concern for pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale. Clarify whether the ordered 'chest ultrasound' is intended as a focused cardiac echocardiogram; a routine chest/pleural ultrasound cannot reliably assess pulmonary artery pressures or diagnose sleep apnea.
must_include_findings: If cardiac ultrasound intended: RV size, wall thickness, and systolic function; right atrial size

Estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure from tricuspid regurgitation velocity, if measurable, and other signs of pulmonary hypertension including septal flattening and pulmonary artery enlargement
IVC diameter and respiratory variation/estimated right atrial pressure; evidence of right-sided volume overload
LV systolic/diastolic function and clinically significant valvular abnormalities as alternative causes of elevated pulmonary pressures
If limited to pleural/chest ultrasound: pleural effusions or other accessible chest abnormalities; state that this examination cannot establish pulmonary hypertension or sleep apnea

differential.diagnosis: Pulmonary hypertension due to chronic hypoxemia/sleep-disordered breathing
Left-heart disease contributing to pulmonary hypertension

submission.clinical_question: Does echocardiography confirm hemodynamically significant aortic coarctation causing neonatal heart failure and respiratory distress, and what are the associated cardiac and ductal findings?
submission.pre_read_summary: Term male infant with VACTERL association, known coarctation and prior TEF/esophageal atresia repair, presenting with tachypnea (RR 60), poor feeding, lethargy and mild hypoxemia (SpO₂ 92%). Femoral pulses are absent, with a systolic murmur and hepatomegaly. Chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings. Prior/current echocardiography describes discrete narrowing of the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, with peak gradient 45 mmHg; receiving alprostadil and furosemide. Ultrasound of chest is likely intended as cardiac ultrasound/echocardiography to evaluate obstruction and its hemodynamic effects.
must_include_findings: Aortic arch/isthmus anatomy: site and caliber of coarctation distal to the left subclavian artery; Doppler peak and mean gradients and diastolic flow continuation
Patent ductus arteriosus: patency, size and direction of flow, including ductal supply to the descending aorta
Left ventricular size, hypertrophy and systolic function; other structural cardiac anomalies
Signs of elevated left-sided filling pressure or pulmonary hypertension; estimated right ventricular pressure and ventricular function
Associated heart failure or pulmonary congestion and presence or absence of pericardial or pleural effusions, if visualized

differential.diagnosis: Coarctation of the aorta with ductal-dependent systemic circulation and congestive heart failure
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
Other congenital cardiac lesion with pulmonary overcirculation
Aspiration pneumonitis or pneumonia associated with feeding difficulties and repaired tracheoesophageal fistula

submission.clinical_question: Does the left lower-extremity venous ultrasound show recurrent deep venous thrombosis, particularly femoral vein thrombosis, as the cause of acute unilateral swelling and pain?
submission.pre_read_summary: 10-year-old boy with homocystinuria and prior lower-extremity DVT presents with 2 days of atraumatic left leg pain, tenderness, and edema. No recent surgery or immobilization. He reportedly has not taken his prescribed pyridoxine, betaine, folate, or aspirin recently. The encounter documents Doppler-confirmed femoral vein thrombus.
must_include_findings: Presence or absence of thrombus and venous compressibility in the left common femoral, femoral, popliteal, and visualized calf veins
Exact location and extent of femoral vein thrombus, including proximal extension if present
Color and spectral Doppler flow and degree of venous occlusion
Associated superficial venous thrombosis or alternative focal soft-tissue abnormality, if visualized

differential.diagnosis: Acute recurrent left femoral deep venous thrombosis associated with homocystinuria

submission.clinical_question: Does the chest radiograph show acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema consistent with transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), rather than hydrostatic edema from transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)?
submission.pre_read_summary: 58F undergoing elective right hip arthroplasty developed abrupt dyspnea and severe hypoxemia (SpO₂ 81% on room air) approximately 45 minutes into intraoperative packed red blood cell transfusion. Bilateral crackles; blood pressure remains normal, without urticaria or wheezing. Assess for bilateral pulmonary opacities and evidence of cardiomegaly or volume overload. Presentation strongly favors TRALI; distinguish from TACO and other perioperative causes of acute hypoxia.
must_include_findings: Presence, distribution, and severity of bilateral pulmonary airspace/interstitial opacities
Cardiac silhouette size and evidence of pulmonary vascular congestion, pleural effusions, or other hydrostatic volume-overload findings
Focal consolidation or aspiration-pattern opacities
Pneumothorax

differential.diagnosis: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) / cardiogenic pulmonary edema
